demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I force myself to think only positive thoughts
I try to push them out of my mind

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be on guard all the time
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination appraisals are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another person; for this trauma type, guilt, responsibility, danger, or moral failure would be more coherent than feeling physically dirty/contaminated, absent any assault or bodily violation context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination conflicts with the trauma type and the rest of the profile: the central event is that he accidentally injured another person, while the appraisals emphasize defectiveness and threat rather than victimization by others. Dwelling on what other people have done to me points to a different trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: Magical thinking that the event did not really happen or was not that bad sits awkwardly with the very high-severity profile and with simultaneous endorsement of full sensory reliving plus strong persistent threat and self-defectiveness. Partial minimization can occur, but this item as phrased is in notable tension with the rest of the profile.

vignette:
# Rajesh's Burden

Rajesh Patel had spent forty-two years in the Coast Guard, most of them stationed along the Maine coast where he had learned to read the water the way other men read books. He was meticulous, methodical, the kind of officer who checked equipment twice and knew every protocol by heart. At seventy-eight, he had retired with a clean record and a pension, and for the first two years of his retirement, he and his wife Priya had traveled—they had seen their grandchildren grow, attended weddings, lived quietly in their home in Portland. Then Priya died suddenly of a stroke, and Rajesh, now eighty and widowed, found himself alone in the house they had shared for thirty-seven years.

The accident had happened on a clear June morning in 1994, during a routine training exercise near Casco Bay. Rajesh was supervising a young ensign, Marcus, who was learning to navigate a rescue boat through shallow water. The instructions had been clear: stay in the channel, watch for rocks. But Rajesh had been distracted—he had just received word that his father was ill in India, and his mind had drifted for perhaps thirty seconds. When he looked back at the instruments, Marcus had already turned the wheel. The boat struck a submerged ledge with a sickening crunch. Marcus was thrown against the console, his arm caught and shattered in three places. The sound—a wet crack like a branch snapping—had lodged itself somewhere in Rajesh's nervous system where it had lived ever since.

Marcus had recovered, eventually. A full investigation cleared Rajesh of wrongdoing; it was ruled a training accident, one of those terrible confluences of inattention and bad luck. But Rajesh had never quite believed the investigation. He had come to understand himself as a man whose moment of weakness had nearly destroyed another person's life, and this knowledge had calcified into a certainty: there was something fundamentally defective about him, a flaw in his character that made him dangerous. Even now, decades later, he carried the conviction that he was the sort of man who could hurt people, that his nature was corrupted in some essential way.

For years after the accident, Rajesh had managed by staying busy. Work had been his refuge—the structure, the protocols, the clear lines of responsibility. But retirement had taken that away. Without the routine of the service, without Priya's presence to anchor him, the old thoughts had begun to surface more insistently. The conviction that he was defective had metastasized into a constant hypervigilance. He had to be on guard all the time now, watching himself, monitoring his actions for signs of the dangerous man he believed himself to be. This vigilance had begun to reshape his life in subtle ways. When he sat in restaurants or his doctor's office, he found himself choosing seats near exits, positions where he could see the room and feel protected from unexpected threats—not because he feared others, but because he feared himself, feared what might happen if he were caught off guard. The constant threat monitoring—the exhausting work of watching himself, of staying alert—kept pulling the fragmented memory back to the surface. On days when his vigilance was highest, when he was most acutely aware of his own potential for harm, the memory of Marcus's shattered arm would surface unbidden, as though the adrenaline itself were dredging it up, making him relive the moment to ensure he never made such a mistake again.

The triggers had multiplied as his sense of danger had grown. Any natural environment similar to the bay where it happened—a rocky coastline, a harbor, even the sound of water lapping against a dock—would send him into a state of high alert. Each time he heard a siren or caught the smell of salt water, the thought would arrive with crushing certainty: this is what happens when you let your guard down, this is the kind of man you are. The trigger did not simply remind him of the accident; it told him something about himself—that he was the sort of person whose carelessness could destroy another life, that vigilance was the only thing standing between him and catastrophe. His body would tense, his breath would shallow. Talking about the future triggered something equally potent; when his daughter mentioned visiting next summer or asked him to make plans, a cold dread would settle in his chest. He had come to associate forward-thinking with the possibility of causing harm again, as though the future itself were a minefield he was destined to navigate badly. And sirens—the wail of an ambulance or fire truck—would transport him instantly back to that June morning, to the moment when the emergency crews had arrived and he had watched Marcus being loaded onto a stretcher.

When these triggers struck, Rajesh's mind would fracture in a particular way. The memory of the accident would return not as a coherent narrative but as disconnected sensory fragments: the smell of diesel fuel, the metallic taste of fear, the visual flash of Marcus's face contorted in pain. These pieces never quite assembled into a whole. When he tried deliberately to remember what had happened—to make sense of it, to perhaps forgive himself—the memory would slip away, becoming inaccessible, as though his mind were protecting him from something too terrible to fully know. Yet when the memory came unbidden, triggered by a siren or the sight of a rocky beach, it would arrive with overwhelming sensory vividness, feeling completely real across all his senses at once, as though he were living through the moment again rather than remembering it.

To manage these eruptions, Rajesh had developed ways of thinking that felt protective but were slowly poisoning his life. He would tell himself that the event had not really happened, or that it had not been as bad as he remembered—magical thinking that provided temporary relief but never lasted. He forced himself to think only positive thoughts, to reframe the accident as a learning experience, a necessary part of his growth. He tried to push the intrusive memories out of his mind, to suppress them through sheer force of will. These strategies would work for a while, creating a fragile calm. But the suppressed thoughts would accumulate, building pressure, and when they finally broke through—triggered by a siren, or a conversation about his daughter's upcoming vacation—they would arrive with even greater force, more fragmented, more overwhelming. The harder he tried to control them, the more they seemed to control him.

The threat monitoring had become exhausting. Because he could not trust his own judgment—because he was certain that his defective nature made him dangerous—he had begun to avoid unfamiliar places where he could not assess the danger. He would not go to new restaurants, new parks, new neighborhoods. He had stopped accepting invitations to events he did not know well. This avoidance had consequences he had not fully anticipated. His daughter had stopped calling as frequently; his son had stopped inviting him to family gatherings. When his doctor suggested he take up walking for his health, Rajesh had refused, because walking meant going outside, meant potentially encountering unfamiliar terrain where something might happen. Instead, he had begun taking risks in other ways—driving too fast on familiar roads, ignoring his blood pressure medication, eating foods his cardiologist had warned him against. It was as though some part of him had decided that if he was going to be dangerous, he might as well be dangerous to himself.

The cycles had tightened over the years since Priya's death. Each time a trigger activated his fragmented memories, the sensory reliving would feel so real, so present, that it would reinforce his conviction that he was fundamentally defective. This belief would then generate more hypervigilance, more threat monitoring, more careful selection of safe seats and safe routes. The avoidance of unfamiliar places would expand, narrowing his world further. And the maladaptive strategies—the magical thinking, the forced positivity, the thought suppression—would provide brief relief before the cycle began again, each rotation leaving him more isolated, more convinced of his own danger.

It was his daughter who finally pushed him to seek help. She had come to visit last month and found him thinner than before, more withdrawn. When she mentioned her son's wedding next spring, Rajesh had become visibly agitated, speaking in fragments about how he could not be trusted around family events, how something bad would happen if he attended. His daughter had recognized something in his words—a rigidity, a hopelessness—that frightened her more than any specific symptom. She had made an appointment with a therapist and told him he was going, and Rajesh, too tired to argue, had agreed. What he feared most was that the therapist would confirm what he already knew: that he was broken beyond repair, that the defect in him was too fundamental to fix. What he hoped for, though he barely dared to name it, was that perhaps—after eighty years, after decades of carrying this burden—there might be some way to understand that a single moment of inattention did not have to define the entirety of who he was.

violations.explanation: Triggers activate memories and threat responses, but no paragraph explicitly conveys that triggers directly drive or lead to negative appraisals about himself being defective.

Although threat monitoring and memories coexist, no paragraph shows that the sense of threat directly produces or triggers the return of fragmented memories—only that triggers activate both simultaneously.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: Triggers activate memories and threat responses, but no paragraph explicitly conveys that triggers directly drive or lead to negative appraisals about himself being defective.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Threat → Memory: Although threat monitoring and memories coexist, no paragraph shows that the sense of threat directly produces or triggers the return of fragmented memories—only that triggers activate both simultaneously.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
